\begin{theorem}[Local $L^1$ endpoint maximal estimate]

purpose: Complete functional, spectral and graph/localization interfaces in section 4
text:
4. Self-similar blow-up
Fix the pure slow profile of Theorem 3.1, and write
A=A_{*},\qquad\Omega=\Omega_{*},\qquad Q=Q_{A,\Omega}.
All functions and spaces in this section are radial, and constants may depend on the fixed profile. The construction below uses a finite-codimension strategy as in Li [46], together with the stable/unstable semigroup framework of [8]. The evolution is studied around the stationary profile, and localization is implemented by a direct finite-dimensional correction to obtain a finite-energy solution.
In the coordinates of (4), write
u(t,x)=(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}e^{-i\Omega\tau}V(\tau,y),\qquad\tau=\log\frac{T}{T-t},\qquad y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{T-t}}.
The rescaled equation is
(51)
\partial_{\tau}V=\mathcal{A}_{0}V-iN(V),\qquad\mathcal{A}_{0}=i\Delta-\frac{1}{2}y\cdot\nabla_{y}-\frac{1}{p-1}+i\Omega.
The profile satisfies \mathcal{A}_{0}Q=iN(Q) . Hence V=Q+v obeys
(52)
\partial_{\tau}v=\mathcal{A}_{Q}v+\mathcal{F}(v),
Set
(53)
V_{\mathrm{diag}}=\frac{p+1}{2}|Q|^{p-1},\qquad V_{\mathrm{off}}=\frac{p-1}{2}|Q|^{p-3}Q^{2}.
Then the linearized operator \mathcal{A}_{Q} and the nonlinear remainder \mathcal{F} are
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{Q}h
\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}_{0}h-iV_{\mathrm{diag}}h-iV_{\mathrm{off}}\overline{h},
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(v)
\displaystyle=-i\bigl[N(Q+v)-N(Q)-V_{\mathrm{diag}}v-V_{\mathrm{off}}\overline{v}\bigr].
We first translate the asymptotics and nonvanishing of Q into global pointwise bounds for the profile and its derivatives. These bounds place Q in the perturbation spaces used below and ensure that cutting off its tail produces a small perturbation. They also show that the coefficients of the linearized operator decay quadratically, with an additional power of decay for each derivative, as needed for the subsequent spectral estimates.
Lemma 4.1.
There are constants c_{*}>0 and C_{Q,j} such that
(54)
|Q(y)|\geq c_{*}\langle y\rangle^{-\frac{2}{p-1}},\qquad|\partial^{\nu}Q(y)|\leq C_{Q,j}\langle y\rangle^{-\frac{2}{p-1}-j},\qquad|\nu|=j\geq 0.
In particular,
(55)
|\partial^{\nu}V_{\mathrm{diag}}(y)|+|\partial^{\nu}V_{\mathrm{off}}(y)|\leq C_{Q,j}\langle y\rangle^{-2-j}.
Proof.
Nonvanishing and the nonzero leading slow coefficient give the lower bound. Write r=|y| and take the approximation P_{\mathrm{out}}^{(J)} from Corollary 3.5, with the phase of Q , and put w_{J}=Q-P_{\mathrm{out}}^{(J)} . Its equation is
\displaystyle w_{J}^{\prime\prime}={}
\displaystyle-\left(\frac{d-1}{r}+\frac{ir}{2}\right)w_{J}^{\prime}-\left(\Omega+\frac{i}{p-1}\right)w_{J}
\displaystyle+N(Q)-N(P_{\mathrm{out}}^{(J)})-r_{J},
\displaystyle r_{J}={}
\displaystyle L_{\Omega}P_{\mathrm{out}}^{(J)}-N(P_{\mathrm{out}}^{(J)}).
The explicit residual satisfies r_{J}^{(k)}=O(r^{-2/(p-1)-2J-2-k}) . Starting with the bounds for w_{J},w_{J}^{\prime} in that corollary, differentiation of this equation gives w_{J}^{(j)}=O(r^{-2/(p-1)-2J-4+j}) for each fixed j\geq 1 , provided J\geq j-2 . Increasing J proves the radial derivative bounds; smoothness at zero and the formulas for Cartesian derivatives give (54). The coefficient bounds follow by the product rule.
∎
4.1. Functional setting
Recall that s_{c}=d/2-2/(p-1) . For s_{c}<s<d/2 , let
\mathcal{X}_{s}=\dot{H}^{s}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C})\cap\dot{H}^{k_{\star}}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}),\qquad\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}^{2}=\||D|^{s}h\|_{2}^{2}+\||D|^{k_{\star}}h\|_{2}^{2},
where k_{\star}\in\mathbb{N} satisfies
k_{\star}\geq 3,\qquad k_{\star}>\frac{d}{2}+2\|V_{\mathrm{off}}\|_{\infty}.
This ensures (s_{c}-k_{\star})/2+\|V_{\mathrm{off}}\|_{\infty}\leq(s_{c}-s)/2 .
We use its underlying real Hilbert space for the scalar perturbation equation, since \mathcal{A}_{Q} is real-linear. The \dot{H}^{s} representative is fixed by the embedding into L^{2d/(d-2s)} . Equivalently, it is the completion of radial C_{c}^{\infty} in the displayed norm. We record the details of the interpolation estimate that will be used below. For h\in C_{c}^{\infty} and R>0 , Fourier inversion and Cauchy–Schwarz give
(56)
\displaystyle\|h\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\|\widehat{h}\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq\int_{|\xi|\leq R}|\widehat{h}(\xi)|\,d\xi+\int_{|\xi|>R}|\widehat{h}(\xi)|\,d\xi
\displaystyle\leq\left(\int_{|\xi|\leq R}|\xi|^{-2s}\,d\xi\right)^{1/2}\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}+\left(\int_{|\xi|>R}|\xi|^{-2k_{\star}}\,d\xi\right)^{1/2}\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{k_{\star}}}
\displaystyle\lesssim_{s}R^{\frac{d}{2}-s}\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}+R^{\frac{d}{2}-k_{\star}}\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{k_{\star}}}.
Choosing R=(\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{k_{\star}}}/\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{s}})^{1/(k_{\star}-s)} balances the two terms and yields
(57)
\|h\|_{\infty}\lesssim_{s}\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}^{\frac{k_{\star}-\frac{d}{2}}{k_{\star}-s}}\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{k_{\star}}}^{\frac{\frac{d}{2}-s}{k_{\star}-s}}\lesssim_{s}\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}.
Here we used the inequality A^{\theta}B^{1-\theta}\leq\theta A+(1-\theta)B .
Lemma 4.2.
For every s_{c}<s<d/2 , the profile Q belongs to \mathcal{X}_{s} .
Proof.
Fix a smooth radial cutoff \chi , equal to one on |y|\leq 1 and zero on |y|\geq 2 , and set \chi_{R}(y)=\chi(y/R) and \eta(y)=\chi(y)-\chi(2y) . For every R\geq 1 ,
Q=\chi_{R}Q+\sum_{j\geq 1}Q_{j,R},\qquad Q_{j,R}(y)=\eta(y/(2^{j}R))Q(y).
For L=2^{j}R , set g_{j,R}(Y)=L^{2/(p-1)}\eta(Y)Q(LY) . These functions are supported in 1/2\leq|Y|\leq 2 , and (54) gives \|g_{j,R}\|_{H^{k_{\star}}}\leq C_{Q} , uniformly in j,R . Scaling in dimension d yields, for k=s,k_{\star} ,
\|Q_{j,R}\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}=L^{s_{c}-k}\|g_{j,R}\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}\leq C_{Q}(2^{j}R)^{s_{c}-k}.
Since k>s_{c} , the series converges in \mathcal{X}_{s} and locally to (1-\chi_{R})Q , with
(58)
\|(1-\chi_{R})Q\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}\leq\sum_{j\geq 1}\|Q_{j,R}\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}\lesssim_{Q,s}R^{s_{c}-k},\qquad k=s,k_{\star}.
As \chi_{R}Q\in C_{c}^{\infty} , this also proves Q\in\mathcal{X}_{s} .
∎
Estimate (56) gives \|\widehat{h}\|_{1}\lesssim_{s}\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}} . Hence, for k=s,k_{\star} , the inequality |\xi|^{k}\lesssim_{k}|\eta|^{k}+|\xi-\eta|^{k} and Young’s convolution inequality give
\|fg\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}\lesssim_{k}\|f\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}\|\widehat{g}\|_{1}+\|\widehat{f}\|_{1}\|g\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}.
Thus \mathcal{X}_{s} is an algebra:
(59)
\|fg\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\leq C_{s}\|f\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\|g\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}.
Since p is odd, \mathcal{F}(v) is a polynomial in Q,\overline{Q},v,\overline{v} whose terms have degree at least two in v,\overline{v} . Lemma 4.2 and the algebra estimate therefore give
(60)
\|\mathcal{F}(v)-\mathcal{F}(w)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\leq C_{Q,s}\bigl(\|v\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}+\|w\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}+\|v\|^{p}_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}+\|w\|^{p}_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\bigr)\|v-w\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}.
Lemma 4.3.
\mathcal{A}_{Q} generates a strongly continuous group S_{Q}(\tau) . Moreover, for any v_{0}\in\mathcal{X}_{s} , there exists T>0 such that a unique mild solution in C([0,T];\mathcal{X}_{s}) solves (52) with initial data v_{0} .
Proof.
The unperturbed operator \mathcal{A}_{0} generates the group S_{0}(\tau)=e^{\tau\mathcal{A}_{0}} , given by
(61)
(S_{0}(\tau)h)(y)=e^{(-\frac{1}{p-1}+i\Omega)\tau}\bigl(e^{i(1-e^{-\tau})\Delta}h\bigr)(e^{-\frac{\tau}{2}}y),\qquad\tau\in\mathbb{R}.
For k=s,k_{\star} , unitarity of the Schrödinger group on \dot{H}^{k} and \|h(\lambda\cdot)\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}=\lambda^{k-d/2}\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{k}} give
\|S_{0}(\tau)h\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}=e^{\frac{(s_{c}-k)\tau}{2}}\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{k}},
since s_{c}=d/2-2/(p-1) . Thus we have for \tau\geq 0 ,
\|S_{0}(\tau)h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\leq e^{\frac{(s_{c}-s)\tau}{2}}\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}.
For radial C_{c}^{\infty} data, continuity at \tau=0 follows from dominated convergence in Fourier space and continuity of dilations. Density and the preceding locally uniform operator bound extend this to every h\in\mathcal{X}_{s} , proving strong continuity.
Moreover, V_{\mathrm{diag}} and V_{\mathrm{off}} belong to \mathcal{X}_{s} by Lemma 4.2 and the algebra estimate (59). Thus \mathcal{A}_{Q}-\mathcal{A}_{0} is a bounded real-linear operator on \mathcal{X}_{s} . The bounded perturbation theorem yields a strongly continuous group S_{Q}(\tau)=e^{\tau\mathcal{A}_{Q}} , with D(\mathcal{A}_{Q})=D(\mathcal{A}_{0}) . Now we show the local well-posedness of (52) in \mathcal{X}_{s} . Using the Duhamel formula, we consider
(62)
v(\tau)=S_{Q}(\tau)v_{0}+\int_{0}^{\tau}S_{Q}(\tau-\sigma)\mathcal{F}(v(\sigma))\,d\sigma.
Estimate (60) makes \mathcal{F} locally Lipschitz near zero. The local bound on S_{Q} thus makes the equation (62) a contraction on a suitable ball in C([0,T];\mathcal{X}_{s}) for T>0 small, proving local existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence for (52).
∎
For the cutoff \chi_{R} in the proof of Lemma 4.2, the estimate (58) shows that localization is small in \mathcal{X}_{s} . The profile bounds and annular scaling give the estimate for the commutator \|[\mathcal{A}_{0},\chi_{R}]Q\|_{\dot{H}^{k}}\lesssim_{Q,s}R^{s_{c}-k}\to 0 for k=s,k_{\star} . Differentiating (61) on Schwartz data gives C^{\infty}_{c,\mathrm{rad}}\subset D(\mathcal{A}_{0}) . Also, the algebra estimate and (58) imply \chi_{R}N(Q)\to N(Q) in \mathcal{X}_{s} . Since \chi_{R}Q\in D(\mathcal{A}_{0}) and
\mathcal{A}_{0}(\chi_{R}Q)=i\chi_{R}N(Q)+[\mathcal{A}_{0},\chi_{R}]Q\longrightarrow iN(Q),
closedness of \mathcal{A}_{0} yields Q\in D(\mathcal{A}_{0}) and \mathcal{A}_{0}Q=iN(Q) . Thus the profile Q is a mild solution of
(63)
Q=S_{0}(\tau)Q-i\int_{0}^{\tau}S_{0}(\tau-\sigma)N(Q)\,d\sigma.
Consequently, subtracting Q identifies a solution of the full nonlinear equation with the \mathcal{X}_{s} perturbation.
4.2. Spectral theory for the linearized operator
Our spectral analysis follows the strategy of obtaining dissipativity
modulo a compact perturbation; see
[52, 54, 9].
We represent the lower-order energy remainder by a compact operator
using the Riesz representation theorem, in a manner analogous to
the construction in [21].
We use the matrix formulation and the associated
\mathcal{J} -invariance argument; see
[60, 46].Fix s\in(s_{c},d/2) and set \gamma_{s}=(s_{c}-s)/2<0 .
The spectral analysis takes place
on the complex Hilbert space
\mathbf{X}_{s}=\mathcal{X}_{s}\times\mathcal{X}_{s},\qquad\|(f,g)\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}^{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\|f\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}^{2}+\|g\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}^{2}\bigr).
Scalar perturbations are identified with the real-linear subspace
(64)
\iota h=\begin{pmatrix}h\\
\overline{h}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{X}_{s,+}=\iota\mathcal{X}_{s}=\{\mathbf{h}\in\mathbf{X}_{s}:\mathcal{J}\mathbf{h}=\mathbf{h}\},\qquad\mathcal{J}\begin{pmatrix}f\\
g\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\overline{g}\\
\overline{f}\end{pmatrix}.
Thus \iota is a real-linear isometry and \mathcal{J} is an antilinear isometric involution.
Let Ch=\overline{h} and \overline{\mathcal{A}_{0}}=C\mathcal{A}_{0}C=-i\Delta-\tfrac{1}{2}y\cdot\nabla_{y}-\frac{1}{p-1}-i\Omega , with domain CD(\mathcal{A}_{0}) . The matrix linearized operator is
\mathbf{A}_{Q}=\mathbf{A}_{0}+\mathbf{B},\qquad\mathbf{A}_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{A}_{0}&0\\
0&\overline{\mathcal{A}_{0}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}-iV_{\mathrm{diag}}&-iV_{\mathrm{off}}\\
i\overline{V_{\mathrm{off}}}&iV_{\mathrm{diag}}\end{pmatrix},
where the coefficients V_{\mathrm{diag}} , V_{\mathrm{off}} are defined in (53). Now we apply the bounded perturbation theorem as in the argument of Lemma 4.3 to the diagonal group
\mathbf{S}_{0}(\tau)=\begin{pmatrix}S_{0}(\tau)&0\\
0&CS_{0}(\tau)C\end{pmatrix}.
Thus \mathbf{A}_{Q} , with domain D(\mathcal{A}_{0})\times CD(\mathcal{A}_{0}) , generates a strongly continuous group \mathbf{S}_{Q}(\tau) . Direct computation gives
\mathcal{J}\mathbf{A}_{Q}=\mathbf{A}_{Q}\mathcal{J},\qquad\mathbf{A}_{Q}\iota=\iota\mathcal{A}_{Q},\qquad\mathbf{S}_{Q}(\tau)\iota=\iota S_{Q}(\tau).
The first identity holds on D(\mathbf{A}_{Q}) , which \mathcal{J} preserves, and the second on D(\mathcal{A}_{Q}) ; the group identity follows by uniqueness. In particular, the matrix evolution preserves \mathbf{X}_{s,+} and agrees there with the scalar linearized evolution.
Lemma 4.4.
There is a bounded compact operator \mathcal{R}
on \mathbf{X}_{s} such that
(65)
\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathbf{A}_{Q}\mathbf{h},\mathbf{h}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}\leq\gamma_{s}\|\mathbf{h}\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}^{2}+\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathcal{R}\mathbf{h},\mathbf{h}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}_{s}},\qquad\mathbf{h}\in D(\mathbf{A}_{Q}).
The operator \mathbf{A}_{Q}-\mathcal{R} , with domain D(\mathbf{A}_{Q}) , generates a strongly continuous semigroup \mathbf{U} , and
(66)
\|\mathbf{U}(\tau)\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}\to\mathbf{X}_{s}}\leq e^{\gamma_{s}\tau},\qquad\tau\geq 0.
Proof.
We first establish the compactness of the lower-order error terms \mathbf{B}\mathbf{h} in the energy estimate. Let \psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be radial, equal to one on the unit ball, and supported in the ball of radius two. Let h=h_{\mathrm{lo}}+h_{\mathrm{hi}} , where h_{\mathrm{lo}}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\psi(|\xi|)\mathcal{F}h is the low frequency part of h . Since s<d/2 , we have
\|\partial^{\beta}h_{\mathrm{lo}}\|_{\infty}\lesssim_{\beta}\left(\int_{|\xi|\leq 2}|\xi|^{2|\beta|-2s}\,d\xi\right)^{1/2}\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}\lesssim_{\beta}\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}.
For the high-frequency part, we have \|h_{\mathrm{hi}}\|_{H^{k_{\star}}}\lesssim\|h\|_{\dot{H}^{k_{\star}}} . These estimates give the localization bound below. Let \chi_{L}(y)=\chi(y/L) , where \chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(B_{2}) is radial and equals one on B_{1} . For each fixed L , localization maps \mathcal{X}_{s} boundedly into H^{k_{\star}} . Hence, choosing \max\{s,d/2\}<r<k_{\star} , Rellich compactness shows that h\mapsto\chi_{L}h is compact into H^{r} . Since multiplication by any of the factors u\in\{V_{\mathrm{diag}},V_{\mathrm{off}},\overline{V_{\mathrm{off}}}\} is bounded on H^{r} and (\chi_{L}u)h=u(\chi_{L}h) , the corresponding localized multiplication operators are compact from \mathcal{X}_{s} into \dot{H}^{s} .
For the tails, (55) and the same dyadic scaling argument as in Lemma 4.2 give, for u\in\{V_{\mathrm{diag}},V_{\mathrm{off}},\overline{V_{\mathrm{off}}}\} ,
\|(1-\chi_{L})u\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\lesssim L^{\frac{d}{2}-2-s}\lesssim L^{s_{c}-s}.
Together with the algebra estimate (59), this gives
\|(1-\chi_{L})V_{\mathrm{diag}}h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}+\|(1-\chi_{L})V_{\mathrm{off}}h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\lesssim L^{s_{c}-s}\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}.
Since s>s_{c} , the right-hand coefficient tends to zero. Therefore
\mathbf{h}\longmapsto|D|^{s}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{h}\quad\text{is compact from }\mathbf{X}_{s}\text{ into }L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}^{2}).
Now let
\mathcal{C}\mathbf{h}=[\nabla^{k_{\star}},\mathbf{B}]\mathbf{h}.
Each component is a finite sum of terms (\partial^{\alpha}u)\partial^{\beta}h , with u\in\{V_{\mathrm{diag}},V_{\mathrm{off}},\overline{V_{\mathrm{off}}}\} where |\alpha|\geq 1 and |\alpha|+|\beta|=k_{\star} . The localized term \chi_{L}(\partial^{\alpha}u)\partial^{\beta}h is compact into L^{2} by local H^{k_{\star}} control, Rellich compactness, and |\beta|\leq k_{\star}-1 . For its tail, (54) gives:
\displaystyle\|(1-\chi_{L})(\partial^{\alpha}u)\partial^{\beta}h_{\mathrm{lo}}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|(1-\chi_{L})(\partial^{\alpha}u)\|_{L^{2}}\|\partial^{\beta}h_{\mathrm{lo}}\|_{L^{\infty}}
\displaystyle\lesssim L^{d/2-2-|\alpha|}\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}},
\displaystyle\|(1-\chi_{L})(\partial^{\alpha}u)\partial^{\beta}h_{\mathrm{hi}}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\|(1-\chi_{L})(\partial^{\alpha}u)\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\partial^{\beta}h_{\mathrm{hi}}\|_{L^{2}}
\displaystyle\lesssim L^{-2-|\alpha|}\|h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}.
Both exponents are negative because d\leq 5 and |\alpha|\geq 1 . Thus \mathcal{C} is compact from \mathbf{X}_{s} into L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{C}^{2}) as well. It follows that
\mathcal{K}\mathbf{h}=(|D|^{s}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{h},\mathcal{C}\mathbf{h}):\mathbf{X}_{s}\longrightarrow\mathcal{Y}
is compact, where \mathcal{Y} is the Hilbert direct sum of these two L^{2} spaces, with \|(f,g)\|_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|g\|_{L^{2}}^{2}) .
Next we work on the energy estimate. The calculations are first made on radial Schwartz pairs. Differentiating the free-group norm identity following (61) gives
\operatorname{Re}\langle|D|^{r}\mathbf{A}_{0}\mathbf{h},|D|^{r}\mathbf{h}\rangle_{L^{2}}=\frac{s_{c}-r}{2}\|\mathbf{h}\|_{\dot{H}^{r}}^{2},\qquad r=s,k_{\star}.
At the top order,
\nabla^{k_{\star}}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{h})=\mathbf{B}\nabla^{k_{\star}}\mathbf{h}+\mathcal{C}\mathbf{h}.
Because V_{\mathrm{diag}} is real, the diagonal terms of \mathbf{B} make zero real contribution. For any pair of tensors \mathbf{w} ,
\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathbf{B}\mathbf{w},\mathbf{w}\rangle_{L^{2}}\leq\|V_{\mathrm{off}}\|_{\infty}\|\mathbf{w}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.
Our choice of k_{\star} implies
\frac{s_{c}-k_{\star}}{2}+\|V_{\mathrm{off}}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{s_{c}-s}{2}=\gamma_{s}.
Define the bounded isometry
\mathcal{E}\mathbf{h}=(|D|^{s}\mathbf{h},\nabla^{k_{\star}}\mathbf{h}):\mathbf{X}_{s}\longrightarrow\mathcal{Y},\qquad\|\mathcal{E}\mathbf{h}\|_{\mathcal{Y}}=\|\mathbf{h}\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}.
Combining the two derivative levels gives
(67)
\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathbf{A}_{Q}\mathbf{h},\mathbf{h}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}\leq\gamma_{s}\|\mathbf{h}\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}^{2}+\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathcal{K}\mathbf{h},\mathcal{E}\mathbf{h}\rangle_{\mathcal{Y}}.
The free energy identity holds for every \mathbf{h}\in D(\mathbf{A}_{0}) . The estimate for the bounded perturbation \mathbf{B} extends from radial Schwartz pairs to \mathbf{X}_{s} by density. Since D(\mathbf{A}_{Q})=D(\mathbf{A}_{0}) , their combination proves (67) on D(\mathbf{A}_{Q}) .
Use inner products linear in the first argument. The sesquilinear form
\mathfrak{k}(\mathbf{h},\mathbf{g})=\langle\mathcal{K}\mathbf{h},\mathcal{E}\mathbf{g}\rangle_{\mathcal{Y}}
is bounded, since |\mathfrak{k}(\mathbf{h},\mathbf{g})|\leq\|\mathcal{K}\|\,\|\mathbf{h}\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}\|\mathbf{g}\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}} . By Riesz representation, there is a unique bounded complex-linear operator \mathcal{R}:\mathbf{X}_{s}\to\mathbf{X}_{s} satisfying
\langle\mathcal{R}\mathbf{h},\mathbf{g}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}=\mathfrak{k}(\mathbf{h},\mathbf{g}),\qquad\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{E}^{*}\mathcal{K}.
The operator \mathcal{R} is compact because \mathcal{K} is compact and \mathcal{E}^{*} is bounded. In particular,
\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathcal{R}\mathbf{h},\mathbf{h}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}=\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathcal{K}\mathbf{h},\mathcal{E}\mathbf{h}\rangle_{\mathcal{Y}}.
Thus the preceding energy estimate proves (65) directly.
Since \mathbf{A}_{Q} already generates \mathbf{S}_{Q} , bounded perturbation by -\mathcal{R} gives the auxiliary group \mathbf{U} , with generator \mathbf{A}_{Q}-\mathcal{R} and domain D(\mathbf{A}_{Q}) . This yields
\operatorname{Re}\langle(\mathbf{A}_{Q}-\mathcal{R})\mathbf{h},\mathbf{h}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}\leq\gamma_{s}\|\mathbf{h}\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}^{2},\qquad\mathbf{h}\in D(\mathbf{A}_{Q}).
Then
\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{d\tau}\|\mathbf{U}(\tau)\mathbf{h}\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}^{2}=\operatorname{Re}\langle(\mathbf{A}_{Q}-\mathcal{R})\mathbf{U}(\tau)\mathbf{h},\mathbf{U}(\tau)\mathbf{h}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}\leq\gamma_{s}\|\mathbf{U}(\tau)\mathbf{h}\|_{\mathbf{X}_{s}}^{2}.
Gronwall’s inequality and density prove (66).
∎
We recall the following theorem.
Theorem 4.5 ([32, Corollary IV.2.11]).
Suppose that A:D(A)\subset X\to X generates a strongly continuous
semigroup T=(T(t))_{t\geq 0} on a complex Banach space X .
Denote its growth bound and essential growth bound by
\omega_{0}(T) and \omega_{\mathrm{ess}}(T) :
\displaystyle\omega_{0}(T)
\displaystyle=\inf\{w\in\mathbb{R}:\exists M_{w}<\infty,\ \|T(\tau)\|\leq M_{w}e^{w\tau}\text{ for all }\tau\geq 0\},
\displaystyle\omega_{\mathrm{ess}}(T)
\displaystyle=\inf\{w\in\mathbb{R}:\exists M_{w}<\infty,\ \|T(\tau)\|_{\mathrm{ess}}\leq M_{w}e^{w\tau}\text{ for all }\tau\geq 0\},
where \|L\|_{\mathrm{ess}}=\inf\{\|L-K\|:K\text{ compact}\} and \sigma(A) denotes the full spectrum of A . Then
\omega_{0}(T)=\max\left\{\omega_{\mathrm{ess}}(T),\sup_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}\operatorname{Re}\lambda\right\}.
For each real number w>\omega_{\mathrm{ess}}(T) , the set
\sigma(A)\cap\bigl\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}:\operatorname{Re}\lambda\geq w\bigr\}
is finite, and its associated spectral projection has finite rank. In particular, its elements are isolated eigenvalues of A with finite algebraic multiplicity.
By [32, Proposition IV.2.12], compact perturbations preserve the essential growth bound, so
(68)
\omega_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathbf{S}_{Q})=\omega_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathbf{U})\leq\omega_{0}(\mathbf{U})\leq\gamma_{s}<0.
Then in our case Corollary 4.5 gives the following proposition.
Proposition 4.6.
For every \delta>0 ,
\sigma(\mathbf{A}_{Q})\cap\{\lambda:\operatorname{Re}\lambda\geq\gamma_{s}+\delta\}
is a finite set of isolated eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity. In particular, the sum of the generalized eigenspaces with \operatorname{Re}\lambda\geq 0 is finite-dimensional.
We now introduce spectral projections to separate the stable part of the linearized evolution from the finite-dimensional neutral and unstable parts. We denote the stable and unstable projections by P_{\mathrm{st}} and P_{\mathrm{un}} , respectively.
Proposition 4.7.
There are bounded real-linear projections P_{\mathrm{un}} and
P_{\mathrm{st}}=I-P_{\mathrm{un}} , commuting with \mathcal{A}_{Q} and S_{Q} , such
that \operatorname{Ran}P_{\mathrm{un}} is finite-dimensional. For some
\omega>0 and C<\infty ,
(69)
\|S_{Q}(\tau)P_{\mathrm{st}}\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}\to\mathcal{X}_{s}}\leq Ce^{-\omega\tau},\qquad\tau\geq 0.
For every \eta>0 , we also have
\|S_{Q}(-\tau)P_{\mathrm{un}}\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}\to\mathcal{X}_{s}}\leq C_{\eta}e^{\eta\tau},\qquad\tau\geq 0.
Proof.
By Proposition 4.6, there exists \gamma_{s}<-\omega<0 such that the set
\Lambda_{\mathrm{un}}=\sigma(\mathbf{A}_{Q})\cap\{\lambda:\operatorname{Re}\lambda\geq-\omega\}=\sigma(\mathbf{A}_{Q})\cap\{\lambda:\operatorname{Re}\lambda\geq 0\}
is finite and consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity. Let \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{un}} be the spectral projection associated with \Lambda_{\mathrm{un}} , and set \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{st}}=I-\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{un}} . The standard spectral argument (e.g., [8, Lemma 7.11]) gives the closed invariant decomposition
\mathbf{X}_{s}=\operatorname{Ran}\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{un}}\oplus\operatorname{Ran}\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{st}}.
From Corollary 4.5 and (68), we have for \tau\geq 0 ,
\|\mathbf{S}_{Q}(\tau)\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{st}}\|\leq Ce^{-\omega\tau}.
From the definition of \Lambda_{\mathrm{un}} , all eigenvalues have nonnegative real part. Jordan normal form therefore gives, for all \eta>0 and \tau\geq 0 ,
\|\mathbf{S}_{Q}(-\tau)\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{un}}\|\leq C_{\eta}e^{\eta\tau}.
Moreover, since \mathcal{J} from (64) commutes with \mathbf{A}_{Q} , we have
\mathcal{J}(z\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}_{Q})^{-1}\mathcal{J}=(\bar{z}\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}_{Q})^{-1}.
Let \mathbf{P}_{\lambda} be the Riesz projection for \lambda . Then
\mathcal{J}\mathbf{P}_{\lambda}\mathcal{J}=\mathbf{P}_{\bar{\lambda}}.
Since \Lambda_{\mathrm{un}} is invariant under conjugation, we have \mathcal{J}\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{un}}\mathcal{J}=\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{un}} . Thus \mathcal{J} commutes with the projection \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{un}} . Hence \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{un}} preserves \mathbf{X}_{s,+} and induces bounded real-linear projections
P_{\alpha}=\iota^{-1}\mathbf{P}_{\alpha}\iota,\qquad\alpha\in\{\mathrm{un},\mathrm{st}\},
with the required commutation properties.
∎
We record the two spectral directions induced by the symmetries of (1). Phase invariance and time translation give, respectively,
\mathcal{A}_{Q}(iQ)=0,\qquad\mathcal{A}_{Q}\left(-\frac{1}{p-1}Q+i\Omega Q-\frac{1}{2}y\cdot\nabla Q\right)=-\frac{1}{p-1}Q+i\Omega Q-\frac{1}{2}y\cdot\nabla Q.
Indeed, the first identity follows by differentiating the constant phase, and the second one follows by differentiating the blow-up time. They can also be checked directly from the profile equation. The symbol bounds of Lemma 4.1 show that both eigenfunctions belong to D(\mathcal{A}_{Q}) . Hence both directions lie in \operatorname{Ran}P_{\mathrm{un}} , and thus this space has dimension at least two. The construction below selects all neutral and unstable components at once, and therefore requires no separate modulation of the blow-up time or of the constant phase. We do not determine whether the two symmetry modes exhaust this space.
4.3. Stability and localization
The following proposition gives a finite-codimensional stability result for the linearized evolution. This result allows us to construct global solutions to the nonlinear equation.
Proposition 4.8.
For the fixed s and \omega above, and every 0<\mu<\omega ,
there is \epsilon_{0}>0 such that, for every
\xi\in P_{\mathrm{st}}\mathcal{X}_{s} with
\|\xi\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}<\epsilon_{0} , the perturbation equation
(52) admits a global solution v with
v(0)=\xi-\int_{0}^{\infty}S_{Q}(-\sigma)P_{\mathrm{un}}\mathcal{F}(v(\sigma))\,d\sigma
and
(70)
\sup_{\tau\geq 0}e^{\mu\tau}\|v(\tau)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\lesssim\|\xi\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}.
Moreover, for every sufficiently large R , such data can be chosen with Q+v(0)=\chi_{R}Q+g_{R} , where g_{R} lies in a fixed finite-dimensional subspace of radial C_{c}^{\infty} and tends to zero in every H^{m} as R\to\infty .
Proof.
To establish the decay estimate
(70), we follow the classical
Lyapunov–Perron construction; see, for example,
[67, Section 9.2]. We then obtain smooth compactly
supported initial data by a finite-dimensional localization
argument related to the constructions in
[49, 46].
We prescribe the stable component \xi and choose the unstable component to cancel the backward evolution of the nonlinear term.
For \xi\in P_{\mathrm{st}}\mathcal{X}_{s} , solve the equation
(71)
\displaystyle v(\tau)={}
\displaystyle S_{Q}(\tau)\xi+\int_{0}^{\tau}S_{Q}(\tau-\sigma)P_{\mathrm{st}}\mathcal{F}(v(\sigma))\,d\sigma-\int_{\tau}^{\infty}S_{Q}(\tau-\sigma)P_{\mathrm{un}}\mathcal{F}(v(\sigma))\,d\sigma.
Choose 0<\eta<2\mu in Proposition 4.7. We use the norm \|v\|_{\mu}:=\sup_{\tau\geq 0}e^{\mu\tau}\|v(\tau)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}} . For \|v\|_{\mu}\leq 1 , (60) with w=0 gives, since \mathcal{F}(0)=0 ,
\|\mathcal{F}(v(\sigma))\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\leq C_{Q,s}\|v(\sigma)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}^{2}\leq C_{Q,s}e^{-2\mu\sigma}\|v\|_{\mu}^{2}.
Here we used \|v(\sigma)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\leq e^{-\mu\sigma}\|v\|_{\mu}\leq 1 . Hence, for every \tau\geq 0 , we have estimates
\displaystyle e^{\mu\tau}\left\|\int_{0}^{\tau}S_{Q}(\tau-\sigma)P_{\mathrm{st}}\mathcal{F}(v(\sigma))\,d\sigma\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}
\displaystyle\leq CC_{Q,s}\|v\|_{\mu}^{2}\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{\mu\tau}e^{-\omega(\tau-\sigma)}e^{-2\mu\sigma}\,d\sigma
\displaystyle\leq\frac{CC_{Q,s}}{\omega-\mu}\|v\|_{\mu}^{2},
\displaystyle e^{\mu\tau}\left\|\int_{\tau}^{\infty}S_{Q}(\tau-\sigma)P_{\mathrm{un}}\mathcal{F}(v(\sigma))\,d\sigma\right\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}
\displaystyle\leq C_{\eta}C_{Q,s}\|v\|_{\mu}^{2}\int_{\tau}^{\infty}e^{\mu\tau}e^{\eta(\sigma-\tau)}e^{-2\mu\sigma}\,d\sigma
\displaystyle\leq\frac{C_{\eta}C_{Q,s}}{2\mu-\eta}\|v\|_{\mu}^{2}.
For \|v\|_{\mu},\|w\|_{\mu}\leq 1 , the same bounds hold with \mathcal{F}(v)-\mathcal{F}(w) in the integrands and \|v\|_{\mu}^{2} replaced by (\|v\|_{\mu}+\|w\|_{\mu})\|v-w\|_{\mu} . Together with (69) and (60), this makes the right-hand side of the equation (71) a contraction on a ball of radius C\|\xi\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}} in
\left\{v\in C([0,\infty);\mathcal{X}_{s}):\sup_{\tau\geq 0}e^{\mu\tau}\|v(\tau)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}<\infty\right\}.
The contraction mapping theorem therefore gives a fixed point v on [0,\infty) . Subtracting S_{Q}(\tau) times (71) at \tau=0 from the same equation at time \tau yields
v(\tau)=S_{Q}(\tau)v(0)+\int_{0}^{\tau}S_{Q}(\tau-\sigma)\mathcal{F}(v(\sigma))\,d\sigma.
This shows the existence of a global solution to (52), with the decay estimate (70).
Now we work on the localization. For each \xi\in B_{\epsilon_{0}}(0)\cap P_{\mathrm{st}}\mathcal{X}_{s} , let v_{\xi} denote the unique fixed point constructed above for that stable datum. Define the map \Phi:B_{\epsilon_{0}}(0)\cap P_{\mathrm{st}}\mathcal{X}_{s}\to P_{\mathrm{un}}\mathcal{X}_{s} by
\Phi(\xi):=P_{\mathrm{un}}v_{\xi}(0)=-\int_{0}^{\infty}S_{Q}(-\sigma)P_{\mathrm{un}}\mathcal{F}(v_{\xi}(\sigma))\,d\sigma.
The integral converges in \mathcal{X}_{s} by the preceding estimates, and v_{\xi}(0)=\xi+\Phi(\xi) . In particular, \Phi(0)=0 since v_{0}=0 . The same estimates for differences give
(72)
\|\Phi(\xi)-\Phi(\eta)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\lesssim\bigl(\|\xi\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}+\|\eta\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\bigr)\|\xi-\eta\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}.
To localize, choose a finite-dimensional real space F\subset C^{\infty}_{c,\mathrm{rad}} for which P_{\mathrm{un}}|_{F}:F\to P_{\mathrm{un}}\mathcal{X}_{s} is an isomorphism. Density of C^{\infty}_{c,\mathrm{rad}} in \mathcal{X}_{s} ensures such a choice. By (58), (\chi_{R}-1)Q\to 0 in \mathcal{X}_{s} . Now we show that the equation
(73)
g_{R}=(P_{\mathrm{un}}|_{F})^{-1}\left[\Phi\bigl(P_{\mathrm{st}}((\chi_{R}-1)Q+g_{R})\bigr)-P_{\mathrm{un}}((\chi_{R}-1)Q)\right]
is a contraction on a ball in F of radius C\|(\chi_{R}-1)Q\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}} when R is sufficiently large. Denote the right-hand side of (73) by T_{R}(g) . By (72), \Phi(0)=0 , and boundedness of the projections and (P_{\mathrm{un}}|_{F})^{-1} , for g,h in this ball we have
\begin{aligned} \|T_{R}(g)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}&\leq K\|(\chi_{R}-1)Q\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}+K(1+C)^{2}\|(\chi_{R}-1)Q\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}^{2},\\
\|T_{R}(g)-T_{R}(h)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}&\leq K(1+C)\|(\chi_{R}-1)Q\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\|g-h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\end{aligned},
with K independent of C and R . Fixing C>2K and then taking R large makes T_{R} preserve this ball and have Lipschitz constant less than one; its arguments also lie in the domain of \Phi . Its solution satisfies P_{\mathrm{un}}((\chi_{R}-1)Q+g_{R})=\Phi(P_{\mathrm{st}}((\chi_{R}-1)Q+g_{R})) , so v(0)=(\chi_{R}-1)Q+g_{R} lies on the constructed graph and Q+v(0)=\chi_{R}Q+g_{R}\in C_{c}^{\infty} . Since F is fixed and finite-dimensional, g_{R}\to 0 in every H^{m} .
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.1.
Fix 0<\mu<\omega and choose localized data from Proposition 4.8. By (57) and (70), V=Q+v is uniformly bounded and
\|V(\tau)-Q\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim e^{-\mu\tau}.
Its initial datum is smooth and compactly supported. Rewriting the Duhamel formula for v relative to S_{0} and using (63) shows that V solves (51). Higher regularity persists, and the tame product estimate yields, for every integer m\geq 3 for which V(0)\in H^{m} ,
(74)
\|V(\tau)\|_{H^{m}}\leq\|V(0)\|_{H^{m}}\exp\left(\left(\frac{d}{4}-\frac{1}{p-1}\right)\tau+C_{m}\int_{0}^{\tau}\|V(\sigma)\|_{\infty}^{p-1}\,d\sigma\right).
Consequently, a bounded L^{\infty} norm prevents finite-time breakdown and propagates all initial Sobolev regularity. Uniqueness and (74) therefore give V\in C([0,\infty);H^{m}) for every integer m\geq 0 . For any T>0 , undoing (4) gives
u(t,x)=(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}e^{-i\Omega\tau}V(\tau,y).
Therefore,
\left\|(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}e^{i\Omega\tau}u\left(t,\sqrt{T-t}\,\cdot\right)-Q\right\|_{\infty}=O((T-t)^{\mu}),
and hence
\|u(t)\|_{\infty}=(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\left(\|Q\|_{\infty}+O((T-t)^{\mu})\right).
The resulting solution lies in C([0,T);H^{m}) for every m , with smooth compactly supported initial data. Since Q(0)=A>0 , we have \|Q\|_{\infty}>0 , and T is its maximal time of existence. Finally, (54) gives |Q(r)|\gtrsim r^{-2/(p-1)} for r\geq 1 . Therefore,
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|Q(x)|^{\frac{d(p-1)}{2}}\,dx\gtrsim\int_{1}^{\infty}r^{d-1}r^{-d}\,dr=\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{dr}{r}=\infty,
so Q\notin L^{d(p-1)/2} . As V(\tau)\to Q pointwise, Fatou’s lemma gives \|V(\tau)\|_{L^{d(p-1)/2}}\to\infty . Sobolev embedding and scaling invariance yield
\|u(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{s_{c}}}\gtrsim\|u(t)\|_{L^{\frac{d(p-1)}{2}}}=\|V(\tau)\|_{L^{\frac{d(p-1)}{2}}}\longrightarrow\infty,
which completes the proof.

Our aim in this paper is to provide a robust approach for the proof of the asymptotic stability of self-similar profiles.
1.3.1. \dot{H}^{s_{c}+} stability theory
Theorem 1.1 (Finite-codimensional asymptotic stability in \dot{H}^{s_{c}+} ).
Let d\geq 1 , s_{c}\in(0,1) , and b,Q_{b} satisfying (1.5), (1.6), (1.7). Then for any 0<\sigma-s_{c}\ll 1 , there exists a Lipschitz finite-codimensional manifold \mathcal{M}\subset\dot{H}^{\sigma} of initial data
u_{0}=Q_{b}+\varepsilon_{0}
where \|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\ll 1 , such that the corresponding solution to (NLS) blows up at T=\frac{1}{2b} with a decomposition
u(t,x)=\frac{1}{\lambda(t)^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}(Q_{b}+\varepsilon)\left(t,\frac{x}{\lambda(t)}\right)e^{i\tau(t)}
(1.9)
where (\lambda(t),\gamma(t),\tau(t)) are given by (1.3) and
\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}_{x}}\lesssim(T-t)^{\frac{\sigma-s_{c}}{2}}.
(1.10)
Moreover, there exists u_{*}\in\dot{H}^{\sigma} such that
u(t)-\frac{1}{\lambda(t)^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}Q_{b}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda(t)}\right)e^{i\tau(t)}\to u_{*}\quad\mathrm{in}\,\,\dot{H}^{\sigma}\quad as\quad t\to T.
(1.11)
The result reduces the nonlinear asymptotic stability to a linear spectral stability problem. As a corollary, assuming the unstable directions of the linearized operator are generated merely by symmetries of the equation (mode stability), we can obtain the asymptotic stability without losing codimensions.
Assumption 1.2 (Mode stability).
Let d\geq 1,s_{c}\in(0,1) , and b,Q_{b} satisfying (1.5), (1.6), (1.7). Let {\mathcal{H}} be the linearized operator around Q_{b} in self-similar coordinates defined by (1.4)-(1.26). For any 0<\sigma-s_{c}\ll 1 , the discrete spectrum of {\mathcal{H}} satisfies
\sigma_{\rm disc}\left({\mathcal{H}}\big|_{(\dot{H}^{\sigma}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2}}\right)\cap\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z<b(\sigma-s_{c})\right\}=\{0,-bi,-2bi\},
(1.12)
with the corresponding Riesz projections satisfying22
2
They are instabilities generated by phase rotation, spatial translation and scaling symmetry respectively. See Section 6.3 for detailed discussion.
\dim{\rm Ran}P_{0}=1,\quad\dim{\rm Ran}P_{-bi}=d,\quad\dim{\rm Ran}P_{-2bi}=1.
(1.13)
Remark 1.3 (Verification of mode stability).
Proving Assumption 1.2 for certain self-similar profile is an independent linear problem. It requires an exact characterization of unstable spectrum for a non-self-adjoint operator, which is relatively unbounded with respect to (matrix) Schrödinger operators. In our forthcoming work [37], we show this property holds for the slightly mass-supercritical profiles constructed in [2] for d\leq 10 , as expected from the stability result [51].
Theorem 1.4 (Conditional asymptotical stability in \dot{H}^{s_{c}+} ).
Under the same assumption of Theorem 1.1 plus mode stability Assumption 1.2, for any 0<\sigma-s_{c}\ll 1 , there exists \epsilon_{1}\ll 1 such that for all \|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}<\epsilon_{1} , there uniquely exists (\lambda_{0},x_{0},\theta_{0})\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R} with
\displaystyle|\lambda_{0}-1|+|x_{0}|+|\theta_{0}|\lesssim\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}
such that the initial data u_{0}=Q_{b}+\varepsilon_{0}
generates a solution blowing up at T=\frac{\lambda_{0}^{2}}{2b} satisfying the decomposition
u(t,x)=\frac{1}{(1-2b\lambda_{0}^{-2}t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}}(Q_{b}+\varepsilon)\left(t,\frac{x-x_{0}}{\sqrt{\lambda_{0}^{2}-2bt}}\right)e^{-i\left[\frac{\ln(\frac{1}{2b}-\lambda_{0}^{-2}t)}{2b}+\theta_{0}\right]}
(1.14)
with the decaying of perturbation (1.10) and the existence of blowup profile in \dot{H}^{\sigma} (1.11).
Comments on Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.4.
1. Regularity. (NLS) is local-wellposed in \dot{H}^{\sigma} with 0<\sigma-s_{c}\ll 1 , see Proposition D.1, so the evolution makes sense with merely u_{0}\in\dot{H}^{\sigma} . This result is almost sharp in terms of regularity for \dot{H}^{s} spaces, and the critical \dot{H}^{s_{c}} stability is still open.
2. Manifold structure of Theorem 1.1. Let B_{\epsilon_{0}}^{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}:=\{f\in\dot{H}^{\sigma},\|f\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}<\epsilon_{0}\} with \epsilon_{0}\ll 1 , then we construct a direct sum decomposition
\dot{H}^{\sigma}=X_{u}\oplus X_{cs}
(1.15)
with X_{cs} and X_{u} are \mathbb{R} -linear subspaces and X_{u} finite-dimensional, and a Lipschitz map \Phi:B_{\epsilon_{0}}^{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\cap X_{cs}\to X_{u} with \Phi(0)=0 , such that the manifold in Theorem 1.1 can be realized as
\mathcal{M}=({\rm Id}+\Phi)(B_{\epsilon_{0}}^{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\cap X_{cs})+Q_{b}.
(1.16)
Moreover, this manifold is tangential to the center-stable hyperplane B_{\epsilon_{0}}^{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\cap X_{cs}+Q_{b} . See Theorem 6.4 for more accurate formulation.
1.3.2. H^{1} stability theory
The self-similar decay (1.7) makes Q_{b}\notin\dot{H}^{s} of any s\in[0,s_{c}] , which raises the question for the existence, stability and behavior of Type I blowup in the energy space H^{1} .33
3

(i)
Finite-codimensional asymptotic stability:
For R_{1}\gg 1 , there exists a Lipschitz finite-codimensional manifold \mathcal{M}\subset H^{1} of initial data

We define the smooth cut-off function,
\widehat{\mathfrak{X}}_{d}(x)=1\text{ when }|x|\leq\frac{1}{2},\quad\widehat{\mathfrak{X}}_{d}(x)=0,\text{ when }|x|\geq\frac{2}{3}.

\Psi_{d}(y)=\Psi_{p}(y)\widehat{\mathfrak{X}}_{d}\left(\frac{y}{e^{s}}\right)
(1.20)

1.5 Organization of the paper
The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 is devoted to the study of the linearized operator around S_{d},\Psi_{d} , and it consists of the proof of Propositions 2.1, 2.3 and Lemma 2.2, concerning maximality, smoothness of the unstable modes and dissipativity of the linear operator. Section 3 upgrades the linear estimates to nonlinear, bootstrapping the bounds of the perturbation. Finally, the Appendix contains a proof of property (1.16) for the globally self-similar solution, as well as some other properties of the solution and some functional analytic results.
1.6 Notation
Throughout the paper we will use the following convention:
We will use C_{x} (resp. C ) to denote any constant that may depend on x (resp. independent of all the other parameters). These constants may change from line to line but they are uniformly bounded by a universal constant dependent on x (independent of all other parameters). Similarly, we will denote by
X\lesssim Y and by
X\lesssim_{x}Y whenever X\leq CY and X\leq C_{x}Y for some C , C_{x} respectively.
We use \nabla^{l}f for the l -th order tensor containing all l order derivatives of f . In the case where f is a vector (typically f=U ) then \nabla^{l}U is a (l+1) -th tensor. We also denote by |\nabla^{k}f| its \ell^{2} norm. Note that this norm controls all the derivatives accounting for reorderings of indices. For example, we have
|\nabla^{j}f|^{2}=\sum_{\beta\in[3]^{j}}|\partial_{\beta}f|^{2}\geq\binom{j}{j^{\prime}}|\partial_{1}^{j^{\prime}}\partial_{2}^{j-j^{\prime}}f|^{2}.
Thus, we see that |\nabla^{j}f| has a stronger control of the mixed derivatives by a combinatorial number, just because any mixed derivative appears multiple times in \nabla^{j}f as the indices are reordered.
For \beta=(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}...,\beta_{K}) , we let \partial_{\beta}=\partial_{\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}...\beta_{K}} , and \partial_{\beta^{(j)}}=\partial_{\beta_{1},\beta_{2},...\beta_{j-1},\beta_{j+1}....\beta_{K}} (that is, \beta_{j} denotes the j -th component of \beta and \beta^{(j)} denotes the subindex obtained by erasing the j -th component in \beta ).
We will use y as our self-similar variable and we will denote R=|y| for the radius (given that r is reserved, since 1/r is the self-similar exponent of our ansatz). We will denote with \widehat{R} the unitary vector field in the radial direction, that is, \widehat{R}=\frac{y}{|y|}=\frac{y}{R} .

\mathcal{L}_{\Psi,t}=\chi_{2}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})\mathcal{L}_{\Psi}-J(1-\chi_{1}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})),\quad\mathcal{L}_{S,t}=\chi_{2}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})\mathcal{L}_{S}-J(1-\chi_{1}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})),
(2.1)
where J,C_{0} are sufficiently large constant.
We will study the cut-off linearized operator \mathcal{L}_{t}=(\mathcal{L}_{\Psi,t},\mathcal{L}_{S,t}) in the space X , which we define as follows. First, we consider \widetilde{X} to be the space H^{m+1}_{\Psi}(Q,\mathbb{R})\times H^{m}_{s}(Q,\mathbb{R}) where the \Psi,s subscripts make reference to \widetilde{\Psi} (vector field) and \widetilde{S} (scalar field). Q is a cube centered at the origin of length 4C_{0} and we take periodic boundary conditions. We select m to be a sufficiently large integer. We define X to be the subspace of \widetilde{X} formed by (\Psi,S)\in\widetilde{X} such that both U and S are compactly supported on B(0,3C_{0}) . One can thus think of X as a subspace of H^{m+1}_{\Psi}(B(0,3C_{0}),\mathbb{R})\times H^{m}_{s}(B(0,3C_{0}),\mathbb{R}) with the appropriate vanishing conditions at the boundary. Whenever we take Fourier series of (\Psi,S)\in X it should be understood that we do Fourier series on the cube Q .
We put in our space X the standard inner product
\langle(f_{\Psi},f_{s}),(g_{\Psi},g_{s})\rangle_{X}=\int_{B(0,3C_{0})}\left(\nabla^{m+1}f_{\Psi}\cdot\nabla^{m+1}g_{\Psi}+\nabla^{m}f_{s}\cdot\nabla^{m}g_{s}+f_{\Psi}\cdot g_{\Psi}+f_{s}g_{s}\right)
and we obtain the inherited norm
\|(f_{\Psi},f_{s})\|_{X}^{2}=\int_{B(0,3C_{0})}\left(|\nabla^{m+1}f_{\Psi}|^{2}+(\nabla^{m}f_{s})^{2}+|f_{\Psi}|^{2}+f_{s}^{2}\right),
(2.2)
where \nabla^{m}f_{s} is an m -tensor indexed by [d]^{m}=\{1,2,...d\}^{m} containing all possible combinations of directional derivatives. In the case of \nabla^{m+1}f_{\Psi} , we have an (m+1) -tensor since we have an extra index indicating the component of the vector f_{\Psi} .
Similar as in the [9], we have finite-dimension unstable space (Proposition 2.1) and smoothness of the eigenvectors in the unstable space (Proposition 2.3).
Proposition 2.1 ([9, Proposition 1.8]).
For \delta_{g} sufficiently small, m sufficiently large and J defined in (2.1) sufficiently large, the following holds. The Hilbert space X can be decomposed as V_{\rm{sta}}\oplus V_{\rm{uns}} , where both V_{\rm{sta}},V_{\rm{uns}} are invariant subspaces of \mathcal{L}_{t} . V_{\rm{uns}} is finite dimensional and formed by smooth functions. Moreover, there exists a metric B of V_{uns} such that the decomposition satisfies:
\displaystyle\begin{split}\Re\langle\mathcal{L}_{t}v,v\rangle_{B}&\geq\frac{-6}{10}\delta_{g}\|v\|_{B}^{2},\qquad\forall v\in V_{\rm{uns}},\\
\left\|e^{s\mathcal{L}_{t}}v\right\|_{X}&\leq e^{-s\delta_{g}/2}\|v\|_{X},\qquad\forall v\in V_{\rm{sta}},\end{split}
(2.3)
where we use \Re to denote the real part.
Proof.
The proof of Proposition 2.1 is the same as in [9]. It follows from the dissipativity and maximality of \mathcal{L}_{t} in lemma 2.2.
∎
Let X_{K} be the finite codimension subspace of X where the Fourier modes smaller than K vanish, that is
\mathcal{F}(\Psi)(k)=0,\quad\mathcal{F}(S)(k)=0\text{ for }|k|<K.
We have the following lemma:
Lemma 2.2 (Dissipativity and Maximality).
Taking K sufficiently large in terms of J , and J large enough depending on m , there is a universal constant C (independent of m ) such that
\int_{B(0,3C_{0})}\nabla^{m}\mathcal{L}_{\Psi,t}\cdot\nabla^{m}\widetilde{\Psi}+\nabla^{m}\mathcal{L}_{S,t}\cdot\nabla^{m}\widetilde{S}\leq-\|(\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S})\|_{X}^{2},\qquad\forall(\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S})\in X_{K}.
(2.4)
Moreover, there exists some \lambda (depending on m , K and J ) such that \mathcal{L}-\lambda:X\to X is a surjective operator.
Proof.
Here (\nabla\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S}) corresponds to (\widetilde{U},\widetilde{S}) in [9] with the properties of profile (1.16) and (1.15). The only difference is that, since we replace \widetilde{U} by \nabla\widetilde{\Psi} , the cut-off in the definition of \mathcal{L}_{t} (2.1) is performed on (\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S}) instead of (\widetilde{U},\widetilde{S}) .
Both the dissipativity and maximality work in a similar way since the change does not effect the leading order estimate ( \dot{H}^{m+1}_{\Psi}(Q)\times\dot{H}^{m}_{S}(Q) ). All the terms where derivatives enter the cut-off are bounded as error terms, so it is irrelevant if the cut-off is performed at the level of \nabla\widetilde{\Psi} or \widetilde{\Psi} .
The error terms are with lower derivative and can be controlled easily by taking K sufficiently large.
∎
Proposition 2.3 (Smoothness of eigenvectors in V_{uns} ).
Let \delta_{g}\in(0,1) . For sufficiently large \overline{m} , \overline{J} , there exist m,J such that m>\overline{m} , J>\overline{J} and we have that the space V_{\rm{uns}}\subset X defined in Lemma 2.1 is formed by smooth functions.
Proof.
The major difficulty here is the d dimension instead of 3 dimension. Instead of the vector spherical harmonics used in [9]. We use the d-dimension spherical harmonic with
S=\sum_{n}S_{n}(R)e_{n},\ \quad\Psi=\sum_{n}\Psi_{n}(R)e_{n},
where e_{n} are spherical
harmonics in d-dimensions [27]. Different from the compressible Euler, the decomposition here highly relies on the fact that U=\nabla\Psi is divergence free, therefore vector spherical harmonics are not needed.
A similar proof as [9, Proposition 2.11] follows.

2.2 The truncated equation and extended equation
In order to choose the initial data of equation (1.25), let
\displaystyle\begin{cases}\widetilde{\Psi}_{0}=\widetilde{\Psi}_{0}^{{}^{\prime}}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}v_{i,\psi}\\
\widetilde{S}_{0}=\widetilde{S}_{0}^{{}^{\prime}}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}v_{i,s},\end{cases}
(2.5)
where
(\chi_{2}\widetilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\prime},\chi_{2}\widetilde{S}_{0}^{\prime})\in V_{\rm{sta}},
(2.6)
and (v_{i,u},v_{i,s}) is an orthogonal and normal basis of V_{\rm{uns}} . Here {a_{i}} is an N -dimensional vector to be fixed later.
In order to use the linear estimate (Proposition 2.1), we define a truncated equation of (1.25) as:
\begin{cases}\partial_{s}\Psi_{t}=\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\mathcal{L}_{\Psi}(\Psi_{t},S_{t})-J\left(1-\chi_{1}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\right)\Psi_{t}+\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\mathcal{F}_{\Psi}\\
\partial_{s}S_{t}=\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\mathcal{L}_{S}(\Psi_{t},S_{t})-J\left(1-\chi_{1}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\right)S_{t}+\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\mathcal{F}_{S},\\
(\Psi_{t}(y,s_{0}),S_{t}(y,s_{0}))=(\Psi_{t,0},S_{t,0})=\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)(\widetilde{\Psi}^{{}^{\prime}}_{0},\widetilde{S}^{{}^{\prime}}_{0})+\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}(v_{i,\psi},v_{i,s}),\end{cases}
(2.7)
where \mathcal{F}_{\Psi}=\mathcal{N}_{\Psi}+\mathcal{E}_{\Psi}+e^{(4-2r)s}\mathcal{D} and \mathcal{F}_{S}=\mathcal{N}_{S}+\mathcal{E}_{S} are the corresponding terms in (1.25). Notice that \chi_{2}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})\mathcal{E}_{S} and \chi_{2}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})\mathcal{E}_{\Psi} vanishes because both terms vanishes in the support of \chi_{2}(\frac{y}{C_{0}}). Here we have
P_{\rm{sta}}(\Psi_{t,0},S_{t,0})=\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)(\widetilde{\Psi}^{{}^{\prime}}_{0},\widetilde{S}^{{}^{\prime}}_{0}),\quad P_{\rm{uns}}(\Psi_{t,0},S_{t,0})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}(v_{i,\psi},v_{i,s}).
P_{\rm{sta}} and P_{\rm{uns}} are the projections to the stable and unstable spaces of \mathcal{L}_{t} that appears in 2.1. Let us mention that the initial data (\Psi_{t,0},S_{t,0}) is compactly supported since the unstable modes will consist on finitely many compactly supported functions (and therefore P_{\rm{uns}} is always compactly supported).
Let us also note that the truncated equation is not a closed equation. On the contrary, one needs to provide the truncated equation with the forcings \mathcal{F}_{\Psi},\mathcal{F}_{S} , and in particular, to compute \mathcal{N}_{\Psi},\mathcal{N}_{S},\mathcal{D} one needs to know \widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S} . Note also that the initial data of the system is the initial data of the original (extended) equation with the appropriate cut-off.
We will rewrite the truncated equation (2.7) as follows
\partial_{s}(\Psi_{t},S_{t})=\mathcal{L}_{t}(\Psi_{t},S_{t})+\mathcal{F}_{t}
(2.8)
where \mathcal{L}_{t} includes the linear operator with a cut-off and the artificial damping, while \mathcal{F} includes both coordinates of the forcing :
\mathcal{L}_{t}(\Psi_{t},S_{t})=\left(\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\mathcal{L}_{\Psi}(\Psi_{t},S_{t})-J\left(1-\chi_{1}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\right)\Psi_{t},\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\mathcal{L}_{S}(\Psi_{t},S_{t})-J\left(1-\chi_{1}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\right)S_{t}\right)
and
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\left(\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\mathcal{F}_{\Psi},\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\mathcal{F}_{S}\right).
We will study the truncated equation in the space X defined in (2.2).
This setting has the following two fundamental properties. The first one is that \mathcal{L}_{t} has finitely many unstable directions, and the second one that the truncated equation agrees with the original equation for |y|\leq C_{0} .
Now, we state a lemma describing the agreement of the truncated equation with the original system:
Lemma 2.4.
Let (\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S}) be a smooth solution of the original (extended) equation (1.25) for s\in[s_{0},s_{1}] . Then, there exists a solution (\Psi_{t},S_{t}) of (2.8) for s\in[s_{0},s_{1}] . Moreover, both solutions agree for |y|\leq\frac{11}{10}C_{0} .
Proof.
The existence part follows from \mathcal{L}_{t} being a contraction semigroup modulo finitely many modes, together with the facts (\Psi_{t,0},S_{t,0})\in X and \mathcal{F}_{t}\in X .
Let us show that they agree in the indicated region. We define (\Psi^{\rm{diff}},S^{\rm{diff}})=(\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S})-(\Psi_{t},S_{t}) . Since the forcing of the truncated equation is computed from the extended equation, that term cancels, and one obtains
\partial_{s}(\Psi^{\rm{diff}},S^{\rm{diff}})=\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\mathcal{L}(\Psi^{\rm{diff}},S^{\rm{diff}})+\left(1-\chi_{2}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\right)\mathcal{L}(\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S})+J\left(1-\chi_{1}\left(\frac{y}{C_{0}}\right)\right).
If we restrict ourselves to |y|\leq\frac{11}{10}C_{0} , the last two terms are zero due to the cut-offs, and in that region, we obtain
\begin{cases}\partial_{s}\Psi^{\rm{diff}}&=-(r-2)\Psi^{\rm{diff}}-y\nabla\Psi^{\rm{diff}}-2\nabla\Psi_{p}\cdot\nabla\Psi^{\rm{diff}}-2\alpha S_{d}S^{\rm{diff}}\\
\partial_{s}S^{\rm{diff}}&=-(r-1)S^{\rm{diff}}-y\nabla S^{\rm{diff}}-2\nabla\Psi_{p}\cdot\nabla S^{\rm{diff}}-2\alpha S_{d}\Delta\Psi^{\rm{diff}}-2\nabla S_{d}\cdot\nabla\Psi^{\rm{diff}}-2\alpha S^{\rm{diff}}\Delta\Psi_{p}\end{cases}
(2.9)
Furthermore, we can perform an energy estimates in the equation above and defining E^{\rm{diff}}=\int_{|y|\leq\frac{11C_{0}}{10}}|\nabla\Psi^{\rm{diff}}|^{2}+|S^{\rm{diff}}|^{2} we get that
\displaystyle\partial_{s}E^{\rm{diff}}
\displaystyle\leq CE^{\rm{diff}}-\int_{|y|=11C_{0}/10}\widehat{R}\left(\frac{y}{2}+\nabla\Psi_{p}\right)\left(|\nabla\Psi^{\rm{diff}}|^{2}+|S^{\rm{diff}}|^{2}\right)-2\alpha\int_{|y|=11C_{0}/10}S_{d}\cdot\left(S^{\rm{diff}}\nabla\Psi^{\rm{diff}}\right)
\displaystyle\leq CE^{\rm{diff}}-\int_{|y|=11C_{0}/10}\left(\frac{|y|}{2}+\partial_{R}\Psi_{p}-\alpha|S_{d}|\right)\left(|\nabla\Psi^{\rm{diff}}|^{2}+|S^{\rm{diff}}|^{2}\right).
Properties (1.15) and (1.14) ensure that g(y)=|y|/2+\partial_{R}\Psi_{p}-\alpha|S_{p}| is increasing and g(1)=0 . Therefore, g(11C_{0}/10)>0 if we ensure C_{0}>1 . Taking C_{0}<\frac{1}{10}e^{s_{0}} , we also have that |S_{d}(C_{0})|=|S_{p}(C_{0})| . Therefore, as long as 1\leq C_{0}\leq\frac{1}{10}e^{s_{0}} we obtain that \partial_{s}E^{\rm{diff}}\leq CE^{\rm{diff}} and since E^{\rm{diff}} is zero at time zero (the initial data for (\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S}) and (\Psi_{t},S_{t}) coincides for |y|\leq\frac{11}{10}C_{0} ), we conclude that E^{\rm{diff}}=0 . This implies that \nabla\Psi_{t}=\nabla\widetilde{\Psi} and S_{t}=\widetilde{S} in this range of y . Thus, we have that for |y|\leq\frac{11}{10}C_{0} , \Psi^{\rm{diff}}=f(s) for some function f(s) (constant in space) and S^{\rm{diff}}=0 , and we just need to show f(s)=0 .
We evaluate the first equation of (2.9) at y=0 , and use that S^{\rm{diff}}(0,s)=0 with \nabla\Psi_{p}(0)=0 . We get
\partial_{s}f=-(r-2)f(s)
and since f(s_{0})=0 because of the agreement of the initial data, we conclude that f(s)=0 for all s\in[s_{0},s_{1}] .
∎
3 Nonlinear stability
3.1 Choice of parameters
We will choose our parameters as follows:
\frac{1}{s_{0}}\ll\delta_{\rm{low}}\ll\frac{1}{E}\ll\frac{1}{k}\ll\frac{1}{m^{\prime}},\frac{1}{R_{0}}\ll b,\varepsilon\ll O(1)\ll E_{0,0},\ll E_{1,0}\ll...E_{\frac{k}{10},0}\ll E.
(3.1)
Here, b,\varepsilon are small constants that just depend on the profile and m^{\prime},R_{0} are big constants that we use in order to close a low derivative L^{2} energy estimate. This energy estimate uses the compressible Euler structure, so it is able to close by itself except for the quantum pressure term e^{(4-2r)}\mathcal{D} . However, that term carries a small constant e^{(4-2r)s_{0}} that is smaller than any other constant involved, so can be closed using higher derivative estimates where the control is much worse.
k measures the number of derivatives in the higher derivative estimates, and E bounds that norm. The precise structure for NLS requires us to consider different energies E_{l,0} at different levels of derivatives in order to close our bounds. Finally, \delta_{\rm{low}} measures the size of the initial data.
Importantly, none of those constants depends on \delta_{\rm{low}} , s_{0} , E_{l,0} .
m^{\prime} is used in the (3.6) as the order of the low derivative energy estimate.
R_{0} , b are the parameter used to define the weight \beta (3.3) and \phi (3.3).
\varepsilon is used to estimate the decay in (3.4), (3.5), (3.6).
s_{0} is the initial time taken to be sufficiently large, it can depend on all other constant.
\delta_{\rm{low}} is a sufficiently small number used in the definition of initial conditions (3.2) and bootstrap assumptions Proposition (3.1) to bound the decay.
k , E_{l,0} with 0\leq l\leq\frac{k}{10} are used in the (3.8) to control the high derivative bound.

\displaystyle\|\widetilde{\Psi}_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}},\|\widetilde{S}_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\delta_{\rm{low}}^{\frac{7}{4}},

3.2 Linear bounds in the X space
The objective of the subsection will be to show
\|\nabla\widetilde{\Psi}\|_{H^{m}(|y|\leq C_{0})}+\|\widetilde{S}\|_{H^{m}(|y|\leq C_{0})}\leq\delta_{\rm{low}}e^{-\frac{3}{2}\varepsilon(s-s_{0})}.
(3.14)
The last ingredient we need in order to show (3.14) is to bound \mathcal{F}_{t} in X norm. Interpolation Lemma 4.1 (adapted trivially to dimension d instead of 3 ) in the case p=q=r=\infty tells us that the high-derivative L^{2} bounds (3.8) together with (3.4) yield:
|\nabla^{i}\widetilde{S}|\lesssim\frac{E^{i/J}}{\langle y\rangle^{ai}}\left(\delta_{\rm{low}}e^{-\varepsilon(s-s_{0})}\right)^{\frac{J-i}{J}}\qquad\mbox{ and }\qquad|\nabla^{i}\widetilde{\Psi}|\lesssim\frac{E^{i/J}}{\langle y\rangle^{ai}}\left(\delta_{\rm{low}}e^{-\varepsilon(s-s_{0})}\right)^{\frac{J-i}{J}},
|\nabla^{i}\widetilde{S}|\lesssim\frac{E^{i/J}}{\langle y\rangle^{ai}}\left(S_{d}\delta_{\rm{low}}\right)^{\frac{J-i}{J}}\qquad\mbox{ and }\qquad|\nabla^{i}\widetilde{\Psi}|\lesssim\frac{E^{i/J}}{\langle y\rangle^{ai}}\left(\Psi_{p}\delta_{\rm{low}}\right)^{\frac{J-i}{J}}
with a=\frac{1}{10}.
Let us recall that X is the space where we measure the stable modes of \widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S} on a compact support, and it is in a lower regularity norm \dot{H}^{m+1}_{\Psi}\times\dot{H}^{m}_{S} , for m\ll k . Now assuming that \delta_{\rm{low}}\ll\frac{1}{E^{2}} and that k is much larger compared to the regularity of X (space used to measure linear stability), we have that
\|(\mathcal{N}_{\Psi},\mathcal{N}_{S})\|_{X}\lesssim e^{-\frac{7}{4}\varepsilon(s-s_{0})}\delta_{\rm{low}}^{7/4}
(3.15)
With respect to the dissipation \nabla^{m}\left(\frac{\Delta(S^{1/\alpha})}{S^{1/\alpha}}\right) , we start computing:
\frac{\Delta(S^{1/\alpha})}{S^{1/\alpha}}=\sum_{i}\frac{\partial_{i}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}S^{1/\alpha-1}\partial_{i}S\right)}{S^{1/\alpha}}=\frac{\Delta S}{\alpha S}-\frac{(\alpha-1)|\nabla S|^{2}}{\alpha^{2}S^{2}}
and therefore, we can bound
\left|\nabla^{m}\left(\frac{\Delta(S^{1/\alpha})}{S^{1/\alpha}}\right)\right|\lesssim_{m}\sum_{|i|=m+2}\frac{|\nabla^{i_{1}}S|}{S}\cdot\frac{|\nabla^{i_{2}}S|}{S}\ldots\frac{|\nabla^{i_{\ell(i)}}S|}{S}
where |i|=m+2 refers to all multiindices with positive integer entries i_{j} that add up m+2 and \ell(i) denotes the length of the multiindex.
From our bootstrap hypothesis |\widetilde{S}/S_{d}|<\delta_{\rm{low}} (3.4), we know that 2S_{d}\geq S\geq S_{d}/2 . Moreover, interpolating S\leq 2S_{d} with |\nabla^{J}S|\lesssim E/\langle y\rangle^{aJ} , we obtain that
\displaystyle\left|\nabla^{m}\left(\frac{\Delta(S^{1/\alpha})}{S^{1/\alpha}}\right)\right|
\displaystyle\lesssim_{E,m}\sum_{|i|=m+2}\frac{S_{d}^{1-i_{1}/J}\langle y\rangle^{-ai_{1}}}{S_{d}}\cdot\frac{S_{d}^{1-i_{2}/J}\langle y\rangle^{-ai_{2}}}{S_{d}}\ldots\frac{S_{d}^{1-i_{\ell(i)}/J}\langle y\rangle^{-ai_{\ell(i)}}}{S_{d}}
\displaystyle\lesssim\frac{\langle y\rangle^{-a(m+2)}}{S_{d}^{(m+2)/J}}
(3.16)
Taking s_{0} sufficiently large (viscosity sufficiently small), we have that
\|\mathcal{D}\|_{\dot{H}^{m+1}}\lesssim\delta_{\rm{low}}^{7/4}e^{(4-2r)(s-s_{0})}
(3.17)
as well. Lastly, note that \mathcal{E}_{\Psi} , \mathcal{E}_{S} vanish in the region where \mathfrak{X}=1 , so in particular they do not contribute to \mathcal{F}_{t} (since it comes with a factor \chi_{2}(|y|/C_{0}) ). Thus, from (3.15)–(3.17), together with the fact that \chi_{2}\in\dot{H}^{m} and that \dot{H}^{m}(\mathbb{T}) is an algebra (for sufficiently large m ) we have that
\|\mathcal{F}_{t}\|_{X}\lesssim\delta_{\rm{low}}^{7/4}e^{-\frac{7}{4}\varepsilon(s-s_{0})}
(3.18)
Now, taking a stable projection, and using that \mathcal{L}_{t} is invariant on V_{\rm{sta}} , we have that

Using Duhamel’s principle and (2.3), we obtain

Therefore, we first claim that for \delta>0 small enough and \Phi\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} we have \textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} where \theta\in X_{\delta} is the one associated to \Phi by Lemma 4.1. Note that since \textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}=0 and \textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}}) is contained in the range of \textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}} , we obtain \displaystyle\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})(\tau)=\chi(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}}, due to Eq. (4.2). Hence \displaystyle\|\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|\lesssim\frac{\delta}{c}e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau} and, provided c is chosen sufficiently large, this implies \textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\in\mathcal{X}_{\frac{\delta}{4}} . It remains to show the Lipschitz-continuity of \textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}}) for arbitrary \Phi\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} . Hence let \Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} and let \theta_{i} be associated to \Phi_{i} through Lemma 4.1. We proceed in a similar manner as before and therefore first deal with \textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}}) . This yields \displaystyle\| \displaystyle\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{1},\theta_{1},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)\| \displaystyle\lesssim \displaystyle\|\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{1},\theta_{1},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau\textbf{})\| \displaystyle+\|\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)\| \displaystyle\lesssim \displaystyle\delta\int_{\tau}^{\infty}e^{\tau-\sigma}e^{-2\omega_{p}\sigma}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}d\sigma \displaystyle\lesssim \displaystyle\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}, by using the estimates given in Lemma 3.4 as well as the estimate \|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X}\lesssim\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}} which was derived in Lemma 4.1. We further obtain \displaystyle\|\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{1},\theta_{1},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)\| \displaystyle\lesssim|\chi(\tau)|\,\|(\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}-\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}})\textup{{u}}\| \displaystyle\lesssim\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X} \displaystyle\lesssim\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}, due to the Lemmas 2.11 and 4.1. Hence, \displaystyle\|\tilde{\textup{{P}}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{1},\theta_{1},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\tilde{\textup{{P}}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)\| \displaystyle\lesssim\delta e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}} \displaystyle+\delta\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{-\omega_{p}(\tau+\sigma)}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}} \displaystyle\lesssim\delta e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}} again with the help of the Lemmas 2.11 and 3.4. The claim is now established, since the conditions of the aforementioned contraction mapping principle have been established. ∎ 4.3. Variation of blowup time We are now going to develop tools that allow us to solve Eq. (4.5) without the correction term \textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}}) . In order to do so, we first introduce the scaling operator \textup{{v}}\mapsto\textup{{v}}^{T} with \displaystyle\textup{{v}}^{T}(\rho):=\begin{pmatrix}&(T-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}}v_{1}((T-T_{0})\rho)\\ &(T-T_{0})^{\frac{p+1}{p-1}}v_{2}((T-T_{0})\rho)\\ &(T-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}}v_{3}((T-T_{0})\rho)\\ &(T-T_{0})^{\frac{p+1}{p-1}}v_{4}((T-T_{0})\rho)\end{pmatrix} for any \textup{{v}}\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{R}):=\{\textup{{v}}\in(H^{2}\times H^{1}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{R}))^{2}:\textup{{v}}\text{ radial}\} . We do this since, due to transformations we applied to Eq. (1.1), the blowup time is now also showing up in the initial data of Eq. (1.11). Motivated by this, we set \displaystyle\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}):=\textup{{J}}(\textup{{v}})^{T}+\Psi_{0}^{T}-\Psi_{0} for any \textup{{v}}\in H^{2}\times H^{1}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{R}). Further, by setting \textup{{v}}:=(\tilde{f},\tilde{g}) we can rewrite our initial data as \Phi(0)=\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}). Next, we need the following result on U. Lemma 4.2. Let \delta>0 be small enough, c\geq 1 sufficiently large, T_{0}\in[1-\frac{3\delta}{c},1-\frac{2\delta}{c}] and T\in[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}] . Furthermore, suppose \|\textup{{v}}\|_{H^{2}\times H^{1}(\mathbb{B}_{R}^{3})} is sufficiently small, where R=\frac{3\delta}{c}+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}. Then \|\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})\|\leq\delta, for all T\in[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}] and the map T\mapsto\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}):[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}]\rightarrow\mathcal{H} is continuous. Proof. First note that \displaystyle\left|[\Psi_{0}^{T}]_{1}-[\Psi_{0}]_{1}\right| \displaystyle=\kappa_{p}\left|\frac{(T-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}{(1-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}-1\right| \displaystyle\lesssim\left|\frac{T-T_{0}-1+T_{0}}{1-T_{0}}\right|^{\frac{2}{p-1}} \displaystyle\leq\left|\frac{1-T}{1-T_{0}}\right|^{\frac{2}{p-1}} \displaystyle\lesssim\left|c\right|^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}. Further, the same estimate holds true for the other components as well. To continue let \textup{{v}}\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{B}_{R}^{3}) . Then \displaystyle\|\textup{{v}}^{T}\|\lesssim \displaystyle(T-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}-3}\|\textup{{v}}\|_{H^{2}(\mathbb{B}_{T-T_{0}}^{3})} \displaystyle\lesssim \displaystyle\left(\frac{c}{\delta}\right)^{3-\frac{2}{p-1}}\|\textup{{v}}\|_{H^{2}(\mathbb{B}_{R}^{3})}. Lemma 4.3. Assume that the assumptions of Lemma 4.2 hold. Then the equation \displaystyle\Phi(\tau)= \displaystyle\,\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau)\left(\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})-\textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}))\right) (4.6) \displaystyle+\int_{0}^{\tau}\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau-\sigma)\left(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma))+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)-\partial_{\sigma}\Phi_{\theta(\sigma)}\right)\,d\sigma has a solution (\Phi,\theta)\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta}\times X_{\delta} and the solution map T\mapsto(\Phi,\theta):[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}]\rightarrow\mathcal{X}\times X is continuous. Let the assumptions be as in Lemma 4.2. Then, there exist functions (\Phi,\theta)\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta}\times X_{\delta} and a T\in[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}] such that Eq. (4.6) holds with \textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}))=\textup{{0}} . Proof. Denote by (\Phi,\theta)\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta}\times X_{\delta} , the functions associated to T through Lemma 4.3. Further note that \partial_{T}\Psi_{0}^{T}|_{T=1}=C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}\textup{{g}}_{0}(\rho), for some constant C_{p}>0 . Therefore we can rewrite \textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}) as \displaystyle\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})= \displaystyle J(\textup{{v}})^{T}+(T-1)C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}\textup{{g}}_{0}+(T-1)^{2}(T-T_{0})^{2}\textup{{f}}(T) \displaystyle= \displaystyle J(\textup{{v}})^{T}+(T-1)C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}+(T-1)C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}(\textup{{g}}_{\theta(0)}-\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}) \displaystyle+(T-1)^{2}(T-T_{0})^{2}\textup{{f}}(T) with \|\textup{{f}}\|\lesssim 1. As |\theta(0)-\theta_{\infty}|\lesssim\delta , we have that \|\textup{{g}}_{\theta(0)}-\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\|\lesssim\delta and from this we infer that \displaystyle\left(\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})|\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\right)=(T-1)C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}\|\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\|^{2}+O(\frac{\delta}{c})+O(c^{-2}), where each of the O -terms is a continuous function of T . By formalizing the locally constant property, from Corollary 1.7 we derive some weighted L^{2} estimates - Theorem 2.2 and 2.3, which in turn have applications to several problems described below.
Definition 2.1.
Let \alpha\in(0,d] . We say that \mu is an \alpha -dimensional measure in \mathbb{R}^{d} if it is a probability measure supported in the unit ball B^{d}(0,1) and satisfies that
(2.3)
\mu(B(x,r))\leq C_{\mu}r^{\alpha},\quad\forall r>0,\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
Denote d\mu_{R}(\cdot):=R^{\alpha}d\mu(\frac{\cdot}{R}) .
Theorem 2.2.
Let n\geq 1,\alpha\in(0,n] and \mu be an \alpha -dimensional measure in \mathbb{R}^{n} . Then
(2.4)
\left\|\sup_{0<t<R}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}\left(B^{n}(0,R);d\mu_{R}(x)\right)}\lessapprox R^{\frac{\alpha}{2(n+1)}}\|f\|_{2}\,,
whenever R\geq 1 and f has Fourier support in B^{n}(0,1) .
Theorem 2.3.
Let n\geq 1,\alpha\in(0,n+1] and \mu be an \alpha -dimensional measure in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} . Then
(2.5)
\left\|e^{it\Delta}f\right\|_{L^{2}\left(B^{n+1}(0,R);d\mu_{R}(x,t)\right)}\lessapprox R^{\frac{\alpha}{2(n+1)}}\|f\|_{2}\,,
whenever R\geq 1 and f has Fourier support in B^{n}(0,1) .
We defer the proof of these weighted L^{2} estimates to the end of this subsection. Let’s first see their applications. We omit history and various previous results on the following three problems and refer the readers to [13, 14, 23] and the references therein.
(I) Hausdorff dimension of divergence set of Schrödinger solutions
A natural refinement of Carleson’s problem was initiated by Sjögren
and Sjölin [28]: determine the size of divergence set, in particular, consider
\alpha_{n}(s):=\sup_{f\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}{\rm dim}\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\lim_{t\to 0}e^{it\Delta}f(x)\neq f(x)\right\}\,,
where {\rm dim} stands for the Hausdorff dimension.
The following theorem is a direct result of Theorem 2.2 (c.f. [13, 23]). When n=2 , it recovers the corresponding result derived from the sharp L^{3} estimate of the Schrödinger maximal function in D.-Guth-Li [12]. When n\geq 3 , it improves the previous best known result in D.-Guth-Li-Z. [13].
Theorem 2.4.
Let n\geq 2 . Then
(2.6)
\alpha_{n}(s)\leq n+1-\frac{2(n+1)s}{n},\quad\frac{n}{2(n+1)}<s<\frac{n}{4}\,.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.
Denote e^{it\Delta}f(x) by Ef(x,t) , and (x,t) by \tilde{x} .
Since \mathrm{supp}\widehat{f}\subseteq B^{n}(0,1) , we have \mathrm{supp}\widehat{Ef}\subseteq B^{n+1}(0,1) . Thus there exists a Schwartz bump function \psi on \mathbb{R}^{n+1} (we require \widehat{\psi}\equiv 1 on B^{n+1}(0,100) ) such that (Ef)^{2}=(Ef)^{2}*\psi .
The function \max_{|\tilde{y}-\tilde{x}|\leq e^{100n}}|\psi(\tilde{y})| is rapidly decaying. We call it \psi_{1}(\tilde{x}) . Note also that any (x,t) in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} belongs to a unique integral lattice cube whose center we denote by \tilde{m}=(m,m_{n+1})=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{n+1})=\tilde{m}(x,t) .
Then we have
(2.8)
\begin{split}&\left\|\sup_{0<t<R}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}\left(B^{n}(0,R);d\mu_{R}\right)}^{2}\\
=&\int_{B^{n}(0,R)}\sup_{0<t<R}|Ef(x,t)|^{2}d\mu_{R}(x)\\
\leq&\int_{B^{n}(0,R)}\sup_{0<t<R}\left(|Ef|^{2}*|\psi|\right)(x,t)d\mu_{R}(x)\\
\leq&\int_{B^{n}(0,R)}\sup_{0<t<R}\left(|Ef|^{2}*\psi_{1}\right)(\tilde{m}(x,t))d\mu_{R}(x)\\
\leq&\sum_{\underset{|m_{i}|\leq R}{m=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}},}\left(\int_{|x-m|\leq 10}d\mu_{R}(x)\right)\cdot\sup_{\underset{0\leq m_{n+1}\leq R}{m_{n+1}\in\mathbb{Z}}}(|Ef|^{2}*\psi_{1})(m,m_{n+1}).\end{split}
For each m\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} , let b(m) be an integer in [0,R] such that
\sup_{\underset{0\leq m_{n+1}\leq R}{m_{n+1}\in\mathbb{Z}}}(|Ef|^{2}*\psi_{1})(m,m_{n+1})=(|Ef|^{2}*\psi_{1})(m,b(m)).
Also we assume \|f\|_{2}=1 so |e^{it\Delta}f| is uniformly bounded pointwisely. For each m\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} we define
\nu_{m}:=\int_{|x-m|\leq 10}d\mu_{R}(x)\lesssim 1\,.
By (2.8), we have
(2.9)
\begin{split}&\left\|\sup_{0<t<R}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}\left(B^{n}(0,R);d\mu_{R}\right)}^{2}\\
\lesssim&\sum_{\underset{\nu\in[R^{-100n},1]}{\nu\text{ dyadic}}}\sum_{\underset{\nu_{m}\sim\nu}{m\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},|m_{i}|\leq R}}\nu\cdot(|Ef|^{2}*\psi_{1})(m,b(m))+R^{-90n}.\end{split}
For each dyadic \nu , denote A_{\nu}=\{m\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}:|m_{i}|\leq R,\nu_{m}\sim\nu\} . Performing a dyadic pigeonholing over \nu we see that there exists a dyadic \nu\in[R^{-100n},1] such that for any small \varepsilon>0 ,
(2.10)
\begin{split}&\left\|\sup_{0<t<R}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}\left(B^{n}(0,R);d\mu_{R}\right)}^{2}\\
\lessapprox&\sum_{m\in A_{\nu}}\nu\cdot(|Ef|^{2}*\psi_{1})(m,b(m))+R^{-89n}\\
\lesssim&\sum_{m\in A_{\nu}}\nu\cdot\left(\int_{B^{n+1}((m,b(m)),R^{\varepsilon})}|Ef|^{2}\right)+R^{-89n}\\
\lesssim&\nu\cdot\int_{\bigcup_{m\in A_{\nu}}B^{n+1}((m,b(m)),R^{\varepsilon})}|Ef|^{2}+R^{-89n}.\end{split}
Consider the set X_{\nu}=\bigcup_{m\in A_{\nu}}B^{n+1}((m,b(m)),R^{\varepsilon}) . It is a union of a collection of distinct R^{\varepsilon} -balls and at the same time, it is also a union of unit balls. These balls’ projection onto the (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) -plane are essentially disjoint (a point can be covered \lesssim R^{\varepsilon} times). For every r>R^{2\varepsilon} by the definition of A_{\nu} , the intersection of X_{\nu} and any r -ball can be contained in no more than R^{10n\varepsilon}\nu^{-1}r^{\alpha} disjoint R^{\varepsilon} -balls. Hence we can apply Corollary 1.7 to X_{\nu} with \gamma\lesssim R^{100n\varepsilon}\nu^{-1} and \alpha . With (2.10) this gives
(2.11)
\left\|\sup_{0<t<R}|e^{it\Delta}f|\right\|_{L^{2}\left(B^{n}(0,R);d\mu_{R}\right)}^{2}\lessapprox\nu^{\frac{n-1}{n+1}}R^{\frac{\alpha}{n+1}}\|f\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim R^{\frac{\alpha}{n+1}}\|f\|_{2}^{2}.
This concludes the proof.
